analysis.one_liner: Lets workers divert their Social Security payroll taxes into private investment accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2004 and sent to its Social Security subcommittee in August, it sat there until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let workers born in 1950 or later opt out of traditional Social Security and put 100% of the 6.2% employee payroll contribution into individual investment accounts, run through government-selected asset managers, banks, credit unions, and mutual funds, and converted to annuities at retirement. Workers born after 1983 would be enrolled automatically. To help pay for it, the bill would cut future benefits for people who stay in the traditional system by switching the benefit formula from wage growth indexing to slower-growing inflation indexing, and would order the Treasury to backfill the Social Security trust funds from general federal revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who elect participation would own an individual account they control, could leave the balance to heirs, and would get a 'recognition bond' preserving the value of benefits they had already earned. Participants who do well in the markets could retire early once their account can buy an annuity paying at least 120% of the poverty line. The biggest institutional winner would be the financial industry: the bill requires professional asset managers for the pooled funds, lets banks, credit unions, and regulated mutual funds serve as account trustees, and certifies insurers to sell the retirement annuities — with management fees paid out of workers' account balances.

how_it_helps.text: Workers who opt in would have 100% of their 6.2% employee Social Security contribution redirected into an individually owned account, invested first in a conservative fund, then in a fund whose default option is 60% stocks and 40% bonds, and after the balance passes $10,000 they could open a self-directed Tier III account.

Participants would receive a recognition bond — a Treasury obligation equal to the value of the Social Security benefits they had already accrued — so opting in would not wipe out benefits earned before the switch.
Retirees whose account balance is too small to buy an annuity paying 120% of the poverty line would get a supplemental minimum benefit payment from the Treasury general fund.

Account balances, annuity payments, and recognition bond proceeds would be exempt from federal income tax, and balances would pass to designated beneficiaries or the estate as lump sums when a participant dies.
Participants could retire early once their account could fund an annuity paying at least 120% of the poverty line.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who stay in the traditional system would bear a benefit cut: the bill changes the benefit formula for everyone else from wage-indexing to CPI-indexing, and because prices rise more slowly than wages, benefits shrink over time. Taxpayers generally would pay for the transition: diverting 100% of employee contributions drains the trust funds, and the bill orders automatic general-fund appropriations to keep the trust funds at full balance. Participants themselves would pay asset-manager, trustee, and annuity fees out of their accounts and would bear market losses, with the only floor being the 120%-of-poverty supplemental payment.

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces wage indexing with CPI indexing for everyone else's benefits — for non-disabled beneficiaries reaching age 62 in 2012 or later — and because the CPI grows more slowly than wages, this steadily shrinks guaranteed benefits year after year.

Diverting 100% of employee contributions would leave the trust funds short, and the bill responds by writing the Treasury a blank check: a standing general-fund appropriation of 'such sums as may be necessary' to keep the trust funds at full balance, a cost that would otherwise require new revenue or borrowing.

Participants would carry market risk on money that used to be a guaranteed benefit: the default account is 60% stocks, other accounts can be up to 80% stocks, and the only protection is a supplemental payment to reach 120% of the poverty line — a thin floor compared to a full Social Security benefit.

Management and trustee fees would be deducted from workers' accounts — the bill requires them to be disclosed in semiannual statements — replacing a system that historically runs at very low administrative cost.
Opting in would be irrevocable, and participants would lose credited wages for insurance benefits other than disability, so a bad investment outcome could not be undone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Individual ownership and inheritable accounts are real benefits for workers who opt in, and the supplemental minimum benefit does protect the worst-off participants from destitution. But the bill pays for those benefits partly by shrinking the guaranteed benefit for everyone who stays in traditional Social Security and by backfilling the trust funds from general revenue, while shifting investment risk onto individuals and channeling payroll money through fee-charging asset managers, banks, and insurers. For higher earners with long time horizons the trade could look attractive; for average and lower earners the lost guaranteed benefit and fee drag weigh heavily.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2004, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee and then to its Social Security subcommittee, and died there with no markup and no vote when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Johnson of Texas introduced the Individual Social Security Investment Program Act of 2004 on July 22, 2004, with 14 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced, and on August 3, 2004 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any consideration in the Senate before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The bill would have allowed workers born in 1950 or later to elect to divert 100% of their 6.2% employee Social Security contribution into tiered individual investment accounts, with workers born after 1983 enrolled automatically.

To help fund the transition, the bill would have cut benefits for people remaining in the traditional system by switching benefit indexing from wage growth to the CPI, and would have ordered standing general-fund appropriations to keep the trust funds whole.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Social Security remained untouched — no benefits were cut and no contributions were diverted — and the financial industry did not gain the new stream of fee-bearing accounts the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Sam Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to convert Social Security into a system of individual investment accounts.

for.name: 18 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Campaigned for re-election in 2004 on adding personal investment accounts to Social Security and pushed the idea on Congress afterward, giving the proposal White House-level momentum.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Rep. Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Social Security and never scheduled a markup or brought it to the floor; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 supporters in the House — the sponsor and 18 cosponsors — were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it, and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee never advanced it either.

industries.industry: Asset managers and mutual fund companies
industries.note: The bill would require professional asset managers to invest the Tier I and Tier II funds and would let regulated investment companies serve as Tier III account trustees, routing workers' payroll contributions into fee-bearing private management. Fees would be deducted from workers' account balances, replacing a program historically run at very low administrative cost.

Insurers certified by the new Board would sell the annuities that retirees convert their balances into at retirement, gaining a large new customer base. Annuities do guarantee lifetime income for workers, but the price includes the insurer's margin.
Banks and insured credit unions would be among the eligible trustees for self-directed Tier III accounts, earning trustee and administration fees on workers' balances.
